title: Microeconomics: the study of individual choices

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define microeconomics, recognise the kinds of question it asks - the choices of individual households, firms and particular markets - and identify its decision makers: consumers, workers and producers.
blocks.repair_note: coverage gaps filled from syllabus guidance

blocks.heading: The small pieces, one at a time
blocks.text: Microeconomics is the study of economic choices at the level of the individual unit: one household, one firm, one market. It asks how a household in Katutura divides a N$3 200 monthly income between rent, food and transport, how Otjiwa Dairy sets the price of a litre of milk, and how many guides Etosha Gate Lodge employs in peak season. The thread running through these questions is that each concerns a single decision-maker or a single market: the price of one good, the output of one firm, the jobs of one workplace. A coffee farmer in Vietnam deciding whether to plant two more hectares faces the same kind of question: her farm, her budget, her market. Microeconomics looks at the small pieces of the economy one piece at a time.

blocks.heading: One firm's price, one firm's question
blocks.text: Kaoko Juice bottles 4 000 bottles a month in Opuwo and sells each at N$12. It weighs raising the price to N$14, expecting to sell 3 600 bottles a month at the higher price. This is a microeconomic decision because it belongs to one firm selling in one market: the objects of study are the firm's price, the firm's quantity and the firm's 9 workers. A macroeconomist leaves this bottle aside and studies the economy as a whole instead: the general level of prices across the country, the total output of goods and services, and total employment. Same economy, different lens: the close-up on one unit versus the wide view of the totals.

blocks.heading: The decision makers in microeconomics
blocks.text:
Microeconomics follows the decisions of consumers, workers and producers. Consumers, often grouped as households, decide what to buy with their income and how much of it to save: a family in Katutura choosing between a bag of maize meal and a taxi fare is taking a consumer decision. Workers decide whether to work, for whom, for how many hours and whether to train for a better-paid job: a mechanic in Ondangwa weighing a job offer in Windhoek is taking a worker decision. Producers, also called firms, decide what to produce, how much, by what method, how many people to employ and what price to charge: Kaoko Juice choosing between N$12 and N$14 a bottle is taking a producer decision.

The same person can play more than one part. The mechanic is a worker when he chooses his job and a consumer when he spends his wages. What makes each of these decisions microeconomic is that it is taken by one decision maker for itself, in a particular market, and its first effect lands on that decision maker and the people it trades with.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The demand and supply analysis of topic 2.2 is microeconomics at work, because it prices a single market; the cost analysis of topic 3.7 stays micro too, following one firm's books.
